props.title: Boot Polish
props.initialSlug: Orphaned siblings fight poverty through bootpolishing

sections.content: Boot Polish stands as a pivotal neo-realist Indian film that revolutionized how childhood poverty was portrayed in South Asian cinema. Following siblings John and Belu, forced to beg on Mumbai's unforgiving streets, the film shares DNA with Italian neorealist classics like Bicycle Thieves (1948) and Shoeshine (1946). Director Prakash Arora, under Raj Kapoor's production banner, crafted raw scenes of street life that influenced later works like Salaam Bombay! (1988) and Slumdog Millionaire (2008).

sections.content: The film's revolutionary approach to depicting child performers set new standards in Indian cinema. Baby Naaz's performance as Belu earned unprecedented acclaim, paving the way for more realistic child acting in films like Apur Sansar (1959) and Masoom (1983). The movie's unflinching look at urban poverty challenged Bollywood's typically glamorized narratives, establishing a parallel cinema movement that would flourish in the 1970s and 80s.

The songs in Boot Polish, particularly "Nanhe Munhe Bachche," became anthems of resilience, influencing how music was used in serious social commentary films. Unlike contemporary melodramas, the film's musical numbers emerged organically from street situations, creating a template followed by later works like Mandi (1983) and Chakra (1981). sections.content: Boot Polish marked a crucial shift from the mythological and romantic films dominating Indian screens. Its gritty portrayal of street life influenced directors like Satyajit Ray and Shyam Benegal, who would later create landmark social realist films like Pather Panchali (1955) and Ankur (1974). The film's focus on economic inequality and child labor created a blueprint for issue-based cinema that continues through contemporary works like Chillar Party (2011) and Stanley Ka Dabba (2011).
